questions.explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the highest isolation level, completely eliminating phantom reads using predicate or index locks.

questions.questionText: Checkpointing in DBMS transaction log management is used to:
questions.explanation: Checkpoints write dirty buffer pool pages to disk and write a checkpoint record, bounding recovery work.

options.optionText: Reduce log scanning time during crash recovery

questions.questionText: During ARIES recovery, which phase scans the log forward from the earliest unwritten dirty page to reconstruct system state?
questions.explanation: The Redo phase re-applies all logged changes (repeating history) up to the crash point.

questions.questionText: During ARIES recovery, which phase scans the log backward to rollback changes of active uncommitted transactions?
questions.explanation: The Undo phase reverses the operations of all transactions that were active (uncommitted) at crash time.

questions.questionText: A schedule in which each transaction reads only values written by transactions that have already committed is:
questions.explanation: Cascadeless schedules avoid cascading aborts by disallowing reads of uncommitted data.

questions.questionText: Which SQL clause is used to sort query output rows in descending order?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY column_name DESC sorts output from highest to lowest.

questions.questionText: What is the default sort order of the SQL ORDER BY clause if neither ASC nor DESC is specified?
questions.explanation: Ascending (ASC) is the default sort order in SQL.

questions.questionText: Which constraint checks that a column value satisfies a specific boolean mathematical condition?
questions.explanation: CHECK constraint validates expressions: CHECK (Age >= 18).

questions.questionText: Can a relational database table have multiple UNIQUE constraints?
questions.explanation: A table can have only one Primary Key, but multiple columns or column combinations can be declared UNIQUE.

options.optionText: Yes, multiple columns can have individual UNIQUE constraints
Only if primary key is absent

questions.questionText: What is a surrogate key in database design?
questions.explanation: A surrogate key is an artificially generated sequential or UUID integer with no intrinsic business meaning.

options.optionText: An artificial numeric primary key generated by the system (e.g., Auto-Increment ID)

questions.questionText: In an E-R model, specialization is a:
questions.explanation: Specialization is a top-down process of creating sub-entity sets from a higher-level general entity set.

questions.questionText: In an E-R model, generalization is a:
questions.explanation: Generalization synthesizes multiple entity sets with common features into a higher-level superclass entity.

questions.questionText: A relation in which all functional dependencies are of the form X -> Y where X is a candidate key is in:
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant X in non-trivial dependencies to be a candidate/super key.

testsWithQuestions.title: BCA-502 Java: 100 Questions Complete Subject Exam
testsWithQuestions.description: Full 100-question exam covering JVM internals, bytecode, OOP principles, interfaces, package scoping, checked/unchecked exceptions, multithreading, synchronization, applet lifecycle, JDBC, and dynamic web design.

questions.questionText: Which component of the Java platform is responsible for loading, verifying, and executing compiled bytecode?
questions.explanation: The JVM loads class files, verifies bytecode integrity, and executes instructions on host hardware.

questions.questionText: Java source code (.java) is compiled into an intermediate architecture-neutral format known as:
questions.explanation: The javac compiler translates human-readable Java code into bytecode stored in .class files.

questions.questionText: Which feature of Java enables the 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) philosophy?
questions.explanation: Bytecode is platform-neutral; any operating system with a JVM port can execute the same .class file.

options.optionText: Compilation into platform-independent bytecode executed by platform-specific JVMs

questions.questionText: The Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler inside the JVM enhances performance by:
questions.explanation: JIT compiles frequently executed bytecode loops into native machine code to dramatically accelerate execution.

options.optionText: Translating frequently executed bytecode hot-spots into native machine instructions at runtime

questions.questionText: Which memory area in the JVM stores class structures, method metadata, and static fields?
questions.explanation: The Method Area / Metaspace stores runtime class definitions, static variables, and method bytecode.

questions.questionText: In Java, all newly instantiated objects and arrays are dynamically allocated memory in:
questions.explanation: Objects reside on the Heap, while local variable references to them reside on the thread call Stack.

questions.questionText: What happens to an object when it is no longer referenced by any reachable thread in Java?
questions.explanation: Objects without active references become eligible for reclaim by the JVM Garbage Collector.

options.optionText: It becomes eligible for automatic Garbage Collection
It causes an immediate memory dump
It is written to virtual swap disk

questions.questionText: Which method in java.lang.Object was traditionally called by the Garbage Collector before reclaiming memory?
questions.explanation: The finalize() method provided clean-up hooks before object reclamation (deprecated in modern Java).

questions.questionText: What is the effect of invoking System.gc() in a Java application?
questions.explanation: System.gc() merely hints to the JVM that garbage collection should run; the JVM decides if and when to do so.

options.optionText: Guarantees immediate and complete synchronous garbage collection
Requests or suggests that the JVM run garbage collection, but execution is non-deterministic

questions.questionText: Which tool in the JDK is used to generate standard HTML documentation from doc-comments (/** ... */)?
questions.explanation: The javadoc tool parses code comments to generate standard HTML API reference documentation.

questions.questionText: Which tool in the JDK is used to disassemble compiled .class files and inspect their bytecode?
questions.explanation: javap disassembles compiled class files to reveal method signatures, constants, and raw bytecode.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a primitive data type in Java?
questions.explanation: String is a reference class type (java.lang.String), whereas byte, boolean, and double are primitives.

questions.questionText: What is the memory size of the 'char' primitive data type in Java?
questions.explanation: Java char is an unsigned 16-bit integer representing Unicode code points (� to ￿).

questions.questionText: What is the default value of an uninitialized boolean instance variable in a class?
questions.explanation: Boolean instance and static fields default to false in Java; local variables have no default and require explicit assignment.

questions.questionText: What is the size and range of the primitive 'byte' data type in Java?
questions.explanation: Java byte is a 2's complement 8-bit signed integer ranging from -128 to +127.

questions.questionText: What is the output of the expression `10 + 20 + "Java"` in Java?
questions.explanation: Operators evaluate left-to-right: 10 + 20 yields 30, then 30 + 'Java' performs string concatenation producing '30Java'.

questions.questionText: What is the output of the expression `"Java" + 10 + 20` in Java?
questions.explanation: Left-to-right evaluation starts with string concatenation: 'Java' + 10 = 'Java10', then 'Java10' + 20 = 'Java1020'.

questions.questionText: Which operator in Java tests whether an object reference is an instance of a specified class or interface?
questions.explanation: The instanceof operator evaluates whether an object reference implements an interface or subclasses a type.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between `==` and `.equals()` when comparing two String objects in Java?
questions.explanation: The `==` operator tests reference identity (same memory address), while `String.equals()` compares text values.

options.optionText: `==` compares character content; `.equals()` compares memory addresses
`==` compares object references (memory address); `.equals()` compares string content
`.equals()` can only be used on primitive types

questions.questionText: Why are String objects considered 'immutable' in Java?
questions.explanation: Once created, the internal char/byte buffer of a String cannot be changed. Any mutation returns a brand new String object.

options.optionText: Because their variable references cannot be reassigned
Because their internal character sequence cannot be modified after creation in memory
Because they can only be used in multi-threaded programs

questions.questionText: Which class should be preferred when extensive string modifications (concatenations) occur in a single-threaded environment?
questions.explanation: StringBuilder provides mutable string operations without synchronization overhead, making it faster than StringBuffer.

questions.questionText: What makes StringBuffer thread-safe compared to StringBuilder?
questions.explanation: StringBuffer methods are decorated with the `synchronized` keyword, preventing data races in concurrent threads.

options.optionText: StringBuffer does not use heap memory

questions.questionText: What will happen if you attempt to access an array index that is negative or greater than or equal to `array.length`?
questions.explanation: Java performs runtime boundary checking and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for invalid indices.

questions.questionText: How is the length of an array determined in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, arrays expose an immutable public field `.length` (strings use the method `.length()`).

questions.questionText: Which loop construct in Java guarantees that the loop body will execute at least once?
questions.explanation: The do-while loop evaluates its termination condition at the bottom, guaranteeing at least one execution.

questions.questionText: In Java switch statements (prior to Java 14), which data types are permitted as switch selector expressions?
questions.explanation: Switch statements support integral primitives (byte, short, char, int), wrappers, Enums, and Strings.

options.optionText: byte, short, char, int, String, and enum types

questions.questionText: What happens in a switch statement if a matching case block omits the `break` statement?
questions.explanation: Omitting break results in fall-through behavior, executing subsequent case statements sequentially.

options.optionText: Execution falls through into the subsequent case blocks until a break or switch end

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used to terminate the current loop iteration and jump immediately to the next iteration?
questions.explanation: continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and advances the loop counter to the next cycle.

questions.questionText: What is the index of the first command-line argument in `public static void main(String[] args)`?
questions.explanation: Unlike C/C++ where argv[0] is the program name, Java's args[0] is the first actual user argument passed.

questions.questionText: What is the output of `Math.floor(-3.7)` in Java?
questions.explanation: Math.floor rounds down to the nearest mathematical integer less than or equal to the argument (-4.0).

questions.questionText: A constructor in Java is characterized by which of the following rules?
questions.explanation: Constructors share the class name, have no return type (not even void), and initialize newly created objects.

options.optionText: Must share the exact same name as the class and declare no return type

questions.questionText: If a class does not define any constructor, what does the Java compiler supply?
questions.explanation: The compiler injects a default public no-arg constructor if and only if no explicit constructors are defined.

options.optionText: A default no-argument constructor with an empty body and super() call

questions.questionText: The `this` keyword in Java is a reference variable that points to:
questions.explanation: The `this` keyword refers to the current invoking instance, often used to resolve variable shadowing.

options.optionText: The current class instance invoking the method or constructor

questions.questionText: How can one constructor in a class explicitly invoke another overloaded constructor in the same class?
questions.explanation: Explicit constructor invocation in the same class uses this(...) and must strictly be the first line of code.

options.optionText: Using super() as the first statement
Using this() as the first executable statement in the constructor

questions.questionText: Which keyword in Java is used to inherit all non-private fields and methods from a superclass?
questions.explanation: The `extends` keyword establishes class inheritance: `class Dog extends Animal`.

questions.questionText: Does Java support Multiple Inheritance of classes directly?
questions.explanation: Java disallows multiple class inheritance to prevent the Diamond Problem, providing interfaces instead.

options.optionText: Yes, using commas like `class C extends A, B`
No, Java avoids diamond ambiguity by disallowing multiple class inheritance, supporting it only via Interfaces
Yes, but only for abstract classes

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used by a subclass to invoke an overridden method or constructor of its immediate superclass?
questions.explanation: The `super` keyword calls superclass constructors (`super()`) or overridden superclass methods (`super.method()`).

questions.questionText: What is Method Overloading (Compile-Time Polymorphism) in Java?
questions.explanation: Overloading occurs when methods in the same class share names but have differing argument signatures.

options.optionText: Defining methods with identical names but different parameter lists (type, count, or order) within the same class
Overriding a method in a child class with the identical signature
Calling a method dynamically via reflection

questions.questionText: What is Method Overriding (Runtime Polymorphism) in Java?
questions.explanation: Overriding lets a subclass replace superclass behavior with exact signature and compatible return type.

options.optionText: Writing methods with same names but different parameter counts
A subclass providing a specific implementation of a method already defined in its superclass with identical name and parameter signature

questions.questionText: Can a static method in Java be overridden by a subclass?
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class, not instances. Re-declaring a static method in a subclass hides it rather than overrides it.

options.optionText: Yes, dynamic polymorphism applies to all methods
No, static methods are resolved at compile-time and are hidden (method hiding), not overridden
Only if declared in an interface

questions.questionText: Which modifier prevents a class from being inherited (subclassed) in Java?
questions.explanation: A `final` class cannot be extended by any other class (e.g., java.lang.String is final).

questions.questionText: Which modifier applied to a method prevents that method from being overridden in subclasses?
questions.explanation: Declaring a method `final` prevents child classes from altering its implementation.

questions.questionText: Which modifier applied to a variable makes its value constant and unchangeable once initialized?
questions.explanation: A `final` variable acts as a constant: once assigned, its value cannot be re-bound.

questions.questionText: An `abstract` class in Java:
questions.explanation: Abstract classes serve as blueprints; they cannot be instantiated directly and may contain both concrete and abstract methods.

options.optionText: Cannot be directly instantiated with the `new` operator

questions.questionText: Can an abstract class define a constructor?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes have constructors to initialize their own fields when subclasses call `super()`.

options.optionText: No, abstract classes cannot have constructors
Yes, invoked via super() by subclasses during subclass instantiation
Only if the constructor is private

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used by a class to implement one or more interfaces?
questions.explanation: The `implements` keyword binds a class to one or more interface contracts: `class A implements B, C`.

questions.questionText: In Java 8 and later, interfaces can contain concrete method implementations using which modifier?
questions.explanation: Java 8 introduced `default` and `static` methods inside interfaces to allow backward-compatible API evolution.

questions.questionText: What are the implicit modifiers for all variables declared inside a Java Interface?
questions.explanation: All fields declared in an interface are implicitly `public static final` (constants).

questions.questionText: What are the implicit modifiers for abstract methods declared inside an interface?
questions.explanation: Interface methods without a body are implicitly `public abstract`.

questions.questionText: Which access modifier restricts the visibility of a class member exclusively to its enclosing class?
questions.explanation: The `private` modifier restricts visibility solely to the declaring class.

questions.questionText: What is the default access level of a member in Java when no access specifier is declared?
questions.explanation: Default access (package-private) permits access from any class located inside the identical package.

options.optionText: Package-Private (accessible by classes within the same package)

questions.questionText: A `protected` member in a Java class is accessible to:
questions.explanation: Protected members can be accessed within the same package and by derived subclasses in external packages.

options.optionText: Classes in the same package and subclasses in any package
Only subclasses in the same package
Every class across the entire JVM

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used at the very beginning of a Java source file to place classes into a namespace folder hierarchy?
questions.explanation: The `package` statement must be the first non-comment statement in a source file.

questions.questionText: Which Java package is automatically imported by the compiler into every Java program without an explicit import statement?
questions.explanation: java.lang (containing Object, String, Math, System, Thread) is implicitly imported into every compilation unit.

questions.questionText: What is 'Autoboxing' in Java?
questions.explanation: Autoboxing automatically converts primitives (e.g., int) into wrapper objects (Integer) by calling Integer.valueOf().

options.optionText: Converting reference objects into byte streams
Automatic conversion of a primitive type into its corresponding Wrapper class object

questions.questionText: What is 'Unboxing' in Java?
questions.explanation: Unboxing extracts the primitive value from a wrapper object (e.g., Integer.intValue()).

options.optionText: Automatic conversion of a Wrapper class object into its corresponding primitive type
Removing a class from a package

questions.questionText: Which method is used to parse a numeric String into an `int` primitive in Java?
questions.explanation: Integer.parseInt("123") converts string digits into a primitive int value.

questions.questionText: What will `Integer.parseInt("abc")` throw at runtime?
questions.explanation: NumberFormatException is thrown when a string does not contain a parsable numerical sequence.

questions.questionText: What is the parent class of all classes in the Java class hierarchy?
questions.explanation: java.lang.Object is the ultimate root superclass of every class in Java.

questions.questionText: Which method in java.lang.Object returns a hash code integer value for an object?
questions.explanation: The hashCode() method returns an integer hash value used in hash tables like HashMap and HashSet.

questions.questionText: What is the general contract between `equals()` and `hashCode()` in Java?
questions.explanation: If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must strictly hold true.

options.optionText: If two objects are equal according to equals(), they must produce identical hashCodes
Equal hash codes mean objects must be equal

questions.questionText: Which class in java.lang provides immutable arbitrary-precision integers?
questions.explanation: BigInteger handles arbitrarily large integers with no upper memory boundary.

questions.questionText: Which class in java.lang provides high-precision arithmetic suitable for monetary and financial calculations?
questions.explanation: BigDecimal avoids IEEE 754 floating-point rounding errors, making it ideal for financial logic.

questions.questionText: What does the `intern()` method in java.lang.String do?
questions.explanation: String.intern() checks the String Pool; if present, it returns the pooled reference, otherwise it adds it.

options.optionText: Returns a canonical representation from the JVM String Constant Pool

questions.questionText: What is the result of `"hello" == new String("hello")`?
questions.explanation: The `new` operator creates a separate object on the heap, so memory addresses differ and `==` evaluates to false.

questions.questionText: All exceptions and errors in Java inherit directly or indirectly from which class?
questions.explanation: java.lang.Throwable is the superclass of all exceptions and system errors in the Java language.

questions.questionText: Which category of exceptions is checked by the compiler at compile-time and requires mandatory handling or declaration?
questions.explanation: Checked exceptions (e.g., IOException, SQLException) must be caught in try-catch or declared in `throws`.

options.optionText: Checked Exceptions (subclasses of Exception excluding RuntimeException)

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of an Unchecked (Runtime) Exception in Java?
questions.explanation: NullPointerException extends RuntimeException and is not checked by the compiler.

questions.questionText: Which block in a try-catch-finally construct ALWAYS executes, regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught?
questions.explanation: The finally block executes reliably for clean-up tasks (e.g., closing file descriptors or sockets).

questions.questionText: Under which specific circumstance will a `finally` block NOT execute in Java?
questions.explanation: System.exit() terminates the JVM process immediately, bypassing the finally block.

options.optionText: When System.exit(0) is executed inside the try block
When a return statement is encountered in the try block
When the catch block throws an exception

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the `throw` keyword in Java?
questions.explanation: The `throw` keyword throws an instance: `throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid input");`.

options.optionText: To declare exceptions thrown by a method signature
To explicitly trigger/throw an exception instance in code

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the `throws` keyword in Java?
questions.explanation: The `throws` keyword advertises checked exceptions in the method signature: `void readFile() throws IOException`.

options.optionText: To declare in the method signature which checked exceptions may be propagated to the caller

questions.questionText: Can a single `try` block be associated with multiple `catch` blocks in Java?
questions.explanation: Multiple catch blocks are evaluated sequentially; narrower exceptions must appear before broader superclasses.

options.optionText: No, only one catch block is permitted per try
Yes, and specific subclasses must precede broader superclass exception handlers

questions.questionText: What is the Java 7 'try-with-resources' statement designed to do?
questions.explanation: Try-with-resources ensures that open streams, connections, and files are automatically closed.

options.optionText: Automatically close resources implementing AutoCloseable without an explicit finally block

questions.questionText: How do you create a custom user-defined Checked Exception in Java?
questions.explanation: Custom checked exceptions subclass java.lang.Exception; custom unchecked exceptions subclass RuntimeException.

options.optionText: Create a class that extends java.lang.Exception
Create a class that extends java.lang.RuntimeException

questions.questionText: What are the two primary mechanisms to create a custom Thread in Java?
questions.explanation: Threads are defined either by extending Thread and overriding run(), or implementing Runnable.

options.optionText: By extending java.lang.Thread OR implementing java.lang.Runnable
By extending Object OR implementing Cloneable

questions.questionText: Which method must be overridden to define the execution code for a thread in Java?
questions.explanation: The `run()` method contains the code executed by the thread upon starting.

questions.questionText: What happens if you invoke `thread.run()` directly instead of `thread.start()`?
questions.explanation: Calling run() directly is just a regular method call in the current thread; start() is required to spawn a new OS thread.

options.optionText: A new thread is spawned normally
The run() method executes synchronously within the current calling thread with no new thread created

questions.questionText: Which method causes the currently executing thread to temporarily pause execution for a specified duration in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: Thread.sleep() pauses the active thread without releasing object monitors/locks.

questions.questionText: Which method allows one thread to wait until another specified thread finishes its execution?
questions.explanation: Calling `t1.join()` pauses the calling thread until thread `t1` terminates.

questions.questionText: What does the `synchronized` keyword prevent in multi-threaded Java applications?
questions.explanation: Synchronization enforces mutual exclusion on an object monitor, ensuring thread-safe access to critical sections.

options.optionText: Data races and concurrent state corruption by restricting access to a critical section to one thread at a time

questions.questionText: Which methods are used for inter-thread communication in Java and belong to java.lang.Object?
questions.explanation: wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() belong to Object and must be invoked from within a synchronized context.

questions.questionText: What happens if a thread invokes `wait()` or `notify()` on an object without holding that object's monitor lock?
questions.explanation: Invoking wait/notify outside a synchronized block throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

questions.questionText: What is a Daemon thread in Java?
questions.explanation: Daemon threads provide background services; the JVM halts automatically when all non-daemon user threads terminate.

options.optionText: A high-priority thread that never stops
A background service thread (e.g., Garbage Collector) that does not prevent the JVM from exiting when all user threads finish
A thread that accesses hardware directly
A thread with no run() method

questions.questionText: What is the valid priority range for threads in Java?
questions.explanation: Thread priorities range from Thread.MIN_PRIORITY (1) to Thread.MAX_PRIORITY (10), defaulting to 5.

questions.questionText: What is the fundamental difference between Byte Streams and Character Streams in Java I/O?
questions.explanation: InputStream/OutputStream handle 8-bit bytes; Reader/Writer handle 16-bit Unicode characters.

options.optionText: Byte streams process 8-bit raw bytes; Character streams process 16-bit Unicode characters
Byte streams are for text; Character streams are for images
Character streams do not use buffers

questions.questionText: Which classes form the root abstractions for Character-oriented I/O in java.io?
questions.explanation: Reader and Writer are the abstract base classes for 16-bit character streaming.

questions.questionText: Which class in java.io is used to wrap an underlying Reader and provide efficient buffered reading along with `readLine()`?
questions.explanation: BufferedReader buffers characters for performance and provides readLine() for text reading.

questions.questionText: What marker interface must a class implement to enable object serialization in Java?
questions.explanation: java.io.Serializable is an empty marker interface that authorizes the JVM to serialize instances.

questions.questionText: Which keyword prevents a specific instance variable from being serialized during object serialization?
questions.explanation: The `transient` keyword tells ObjectOutputStream to skip that field during serialization.

questions.questionText: What is the correct execution lifecycle order of a standard Java Applet?
questions.explanation: The Applet lifecycle proceeds: init() on load, start() when active, paint() to render, stop() on exit, and destroy() before unloading.

questions.questionText: Which method in an Applet is responsible for rendering graphical text, shapes, and images using a Graphics context?
questions.explanation: paint(Graphics g) draws shapes, text (drawString), and images onto the applet window.

questions.questionText: In the Java Delegation Event Model, an object that generates an event is called an:
questions.explanation: An Event Source generates events (e.g. Button click) and delivers them to registered Event Listeners.

questions.questionText: Which class in the `java.net` package is used by a server to listen for and accept incoming TCP client connections?
questions.explanation: ServerSocket listens on a port and blocks at accept() until a client connects, returning a Socket.

questions.questionText: Which class in `java.net` represents an IP address and provides domain name resolution?
questions.explanation: InetAddress encapsulates 32-bit/128-bit IP addresses and resolves hostnames via DNS (e.g., InetAddress.getByName()).

questions.questionText: In JDBC, which interface is preferred for executing parameterized SQL queries to prevent SQL Injection and optimize performance?
questions.explanation: PreparedStatement pre-compiles queries and safely binds parameters, neutralizing SQL injection.

questions.questionText: In JDBC, which method of Statement is used to execute a SQL query that retrieves data (e.g., SELECT)?
questions.explanation: executeQuery() returns a ResultSet containing query rows; executeUpdate() is for INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

questions.questionText: In HTML, which attribute of the `<a>` tag specifies the target hyperlink URL destination?
questions.explanation: The `href` (hypertext reference) attribute dictates the destination web page address.

questions.questionText: Which HTML form element creates a drop-down selection list?
questions.explanation: A `<select>` tag containing `<option>` elements generates a standard drop-down menu.

questions.questionText: What is the primary difference between HTTP GET and POST methods in web forms?
questions.explanation: GET sends parameters visible in the URL bar (limited length, cacheable); POST carries data invisibly in the request body.

options.optionText: GET encrypts data; POST does not
GET appends form data to the URL query string; POST sends data in the HTTP request message body
GET can send binary files; POST cannot

testsWithQuestions.title: BCA-503 Networks: 100 Questions Complete Subject Exam
testsWithQuestions.description: Complete 100-question exam covering OSI & TCP/IP models, physical media, HDLC framing, bit stuffing, sliding window ARQ, CRC & Hamming codes, CSMA/CD, IPv4/IPv6, routing protocols (Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford), and TCP/UDP.

questions.questionText: Which network topology connects every computer to a central device such as a hub or switch?
questions.explanation: In Star topology, every node connects via dedicated point-to-point links to a central hub/switch.

questions.questionText: In a Fully Connected Mesh topology having 'n' devices, how many physical duplex links are required?
questions.explanation: A full mesh network requires n(n - 1) / 2 physical bidirectional links to connect all node pairs.

questions.questionText: Which physical transmission medium uses light pulses to transmit data at very high speeds with zero EMI?
questions.explanation: Fiber optic cables carry data as pulses of light guided through silica glass fibers, unaffected by electromagnetic interference.

questions.questionText: What physical phenomenon governs the transmission of light pulses inside an optical fiber core?
questions.explanation: Total Internal Reflection occurs when light strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle.

questions.questionText: Which type of switching dedicates a physical communication path between sender and receiver for the entire session?
questions.explanation: Circuit switching (used in traditional telephony) reserves dedicated end-to-end bandwidth before data flows.

questions.questionText: What is the primary advantage of Packet Switching over Circuit Switching?
questions.explanation: Packet switching dynamically shares bandwidth among active nodes, utilizing transmission capacity far more efficiently.

options.optionText: Dynamic statistical multiplexing and high link utilization efficiency

questions.questionText: Which network category covers a small geographical area such as a single room, lab, or office building?
questions.explanation: LANs operate across bounded geographic areas (homes, offices) typically spanning less than a few kilometers.

questions.questionText: In a Bus topology, what critical component must be placed at both ends of the backbone coaxial cable to absorb reflections?
questions.explanation: Terminators match impedance at the cable extremities, absorbing signals to eliminate signal bounce/reflection.

questions.questionText: Attenuation in computer networking refers to:
questions.explanation: Attenuation is the gradual decay of signal amplitude over transmission distance, compensated by amplifiers/repeaters.

options.optionText: Loss of signal strength and energy as a wave propagates over physical distance
Packet loss due to buffer overflow

questions.questionText: What is the theoretical maximum channel capacity of a noiseless channel according to Nyquist theorem?
questions.explanation: Nyquist formula C = 2B log2(M) gives maximum bit rate for bandwidth B and discrete signal levels M in noiseless media.

questions.questionText: What does Shannon's Channel Capacity theorem define for a noisy channel?
questions.explanation: Shannon's capacity formula establishes the upper transmission bound in the presence of Gaussian thermal noise.

options.optionText: Theoretical maximum error-free data rate: C = B log2(1 + SNR)

questions.questionText: Which unguided (wireless) transmission band is used for television remotes and short-range line-of-sight devices?
questions.explanation: Infrared signals cannot penetrate solid walls and are used for secure, short-range indoor devices and remotes.

questions.questionText: Which transmission impairment is caused by the unwanted electrical coupling between adjacent wire pairs in a cable?
questions.explanation: Crosstalk happens when electromagnetic radiation from one twisted pair leaks into an adjacent wire pair.

questions.questionText: A communication mode where transmission can occur in both directions simultaneously is called:
questions.explanation: Full-Duplex (e.g., standard telephone or switched Ethernet) supports concurrent bidirectional transmission.

questions.questionText: A walkie-talkie where users take turns transmitting one at a time is an example of:
questions.explanation: Half-Duplex allows bidirectional communication, but only one party may transmit on the shared frequency at a given moment.

questions.questionText: How many layers are specified in the standard ISO-OSI Reference Model?
questions.explanation: The OSI model specifies 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Data Link Layer?
questions.explanation: Data Link PDU is a Frame; Physical is Bit; Network is Packet; Transport is Segment.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Network Layer?
questions.explanation: The Network layer encapsulates transport segments into Packets / Datagrams with logical IP addresses.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Transport Layer?
questions.explanation: The Transport layer encapsulates application messages into Segments (TCP) or User Datagrams (UDP).

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer is responsible for end-to-end process-to-process delivery, flow control, and port addressing?
questions.explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides process-to-process communication using source and destination port numbers.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer performs cryptographic encryption/decryption, data compression, and character set translation?
questions.explanation: The Presentation layer (Layer 6) handles abstract data formatting, encoding (ASCII/Unicode), and SSL/TLS encryption.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates dialog sessions between cooperating applications?
questions.explanation: The Session layer (Layer 5) maintains session tokens, dialog control (simplex/half/full duplex), and synchronization checkpoints.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets across interconnected disparate networks using logical addresses?
questions.explanation: The Network layer determines optimal paths across hops using IP routing protocols.

questions.questionText: How many layers are defined in the original TCP/IP protocol suite?
questions.explanation: TCP/IP architecture defines 4 primary layers: Network Interface, Internet, Transport, and Application.

questions.questionText: Which device operates at the Physical layer (Layer 1) to regenerate and retransmit degraded electrical signals?
questions.explanation: Repeaters and hubs operate at Layer 1, regenerating electrical bit streams without inspecting headers.

questions.questionText: A standard Layer 2 Network Switch makes packet forwarding decisions based on:
questions.explanation: Layer 2 switches maintain MAC Address Tables (CAM tables) to forward frames to specific physical ports.

questions.questionText: A Network Router operates at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network Layer) and inspect IP headers to make path routing decisions.

questions.questionText: Which network device connects two distinct network architectures operating on completely different protocol suites?
questions.explanation: A Gateway translates protocols across all 7 OSI layers, bridging incompatible networks.

questions.questionText: What is the size of an IEEE 802 standard MAC (Ethernet) address?
questions.explanation: Ethernet MAC addresses are 48-bit hardware identifiers represented as 12 hexadecimal digits (e.g., 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E).

questions.questionText: What are the first 3 bytes (24 bits) of an Ethernet MAC address known as?
questions.explanation: The first 24 bits are the IEEE-assigned OUI identifying the hardware manufacturer / vendor.

questions.questionText: In HDLC framing, what specific bit pattern is used as the start and end flag sequence?
questions.explanation: HDLC flags use 01111110 (six consecutive ones bounded by zeroes) to delimit frame boundaries.

questions.questionText: What technique does HDLC use to prevent the flag pattern (01111110) from accidentally appearing in payload data?
questions.explanation: Bit stuffing automatically inserts a '0' bit after any sequence of five consecutive '1' bits in the payload.

options.optionText: Bit Stuffing (inserting a 0 after five consecutive 1s)

questions.questionText: In Byte Stuffing (Character-Oriented Framing), which special escape character is stuffed before payload delimiter bytes?
questions.explanation: DLE (Data Link Escape) is stuffed before occurrences of DLE STX or DLE ETX inside data payload.

questions.questionText: What is 'Piggybacking' in data link layer protocols?
questions.explanation: Piggybacking appends acknowledgment numbers to outgoing reverse data frames, conserving bandwidth.

options.optionText: Delaying an acknowledgment (ACK) to attach it to the header of the next outgoing data frame
Compressing multiple packets into one frame

questions.questionText: In Stop-and-Wait ARQ, what happens if an acknowledgment (ACK) frame is lost in transit?
questions.explanation: Timeout expiration triggers retransmission of the unacknowledged frame.

options.optionText: The sender's retransmission timer expires and the data frame is automatically retransmitted

questions.questionText: In a Go-Back-N ARQ protocol with an m-bit sequence number, what is the maximum permissible sender window size?
questions.explanation: To avoid ambiguity between new frames and retransmissions, Go-Back-N sender window size must not exceed 2^m - 1.

questions.questionText: What is the receiver window size in Go-Back-N ARQ?
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N receivers accept frames strictly in sequence, maintaining a receive window size of 1 and discarding out-of-order frames.

questions.questionText: In Selective Repeat ARQ with an m-bit sequence number, what is the maximum sender and receiver window size?
questions.explanation: In Selective Repeat, both sender and receiver windows are equal, with maximum size 2^(m - 1) to prevent sequence overlap.

questions.questionText: Which ARQ flow control protocol retransmits ONLY the specific damaged or lost frame rather than subsequent frames?
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order frames and requests retransmission of only the specific missing sequence number.

questions.questionText: In HDLC, which frame type carries actual user data and piggybacked acknowledgment sequence numbers?
questions.explanation: I-Frames carry payload data along with N(S) send sequence and N(R) receive sequence acknowledgment numbers.

questions.questionText: In HDLC, Supervisory Frames (S-Frames) are primarily utilized for:
questions.explanation: S-Frames contain control commands for flow/error management without carrying payload data.

options.optionText: Flow control and error control (ACK, NAK, Receive Ready RR, Receive Not Ready RNR)

questions.questionText: In HDLC, Unnumbered Frames (U-Frames) are utilized for:
questions.explanation: U-Frames manage link initialization and teardown (e.g. Set Asynchronous Balanced Mode SABM).

options.optionText: Link setup, disconnect, mode setting (SABM, DISC), and reporting unrecoverable errors

questions.questionText: What is the efficiency of Stop-and-Wait protocol when propagation delay (Tp) is significantly larger than transmission time (Tt)?
questions.explanation: High latency satellite or long-haul links make Stop-and-Wait highly inefficient because sender idles waiting for ACKs.

options.optionText: Extremely low: Efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a) where a = Tp / Tt

questions.questionText: What does the parameter 'a' represent in data communication efficiency formulas?
questions.explanation: The parameter a = Tp / Tt measures how many packet lengths fill the pipe during round-trip propagation.

options.optionText: Ratio of propagation delay to transmission delay (Tp / Tt)

questions.questionText: Which data link layer protocol is universally used over direct point-to-point serial links and dial-up/DSL internet connections?
questions.explanation: PPP encapsulates packets over serial links and handles authentication (PAP/CHAP) and IP address negotiation.

questions.questionText: In Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), if the generator polynomial is of degree 'r', how many check bits (zeroes) are appended to the data bits before division?
questions.explanation: A generator polynomial of degree r requires appending exactly r zeroes to data before modulo-2 polynomial division.

questions.questionText: Modulo-2 arithmetic used in CRC calculations is mathematically equivalent to which bitwise operation?
questions.explanation: Modulo-2 addition and subtraction are identical and equivalent to the bitwise XOR operation without carries.

questions.questionText: To detect up to 'd' single-bit errors in any transmission, the minimum Hamming distance of the code must be:
questions.explanation: To detect d single-bit errors, the code words must have a minimum Hamming distance of d + 1.

questions.questionText: To correct up to 't' single-bit errors in any transmission, the minimum Hamming distance of the code must be:
questions.explanation: To guarantee correction of t errors, spheres of radius t around valid codewords must not overlap: d_min >= 2t + 1.

questions.questionText: What is the Hamming distance between the two codewords 1011101 and 1001001?
questions.explanation: Hamming distance is the count of differing bit positions: positions 3 and 5 differ, so distance is 2.

questions.questionText: How does the standard Internet Checksum algorithm verify data integrity at the receiver?
questions.explanation: The 16-bit 1's complement sum of the packet header including checksum must equal 0xFFFF (all 1s).

options.optionText: Sums 16-bit words using 1's complement arithmetic; valid sum of data plus checksum should be all 1s (or 0)

questions.questionText: Which error detection scheme is capable of detecting all odd-numbered bit errors?
questions.explanation: Even parity flips its parity bit on any odd number of bit errors, guaranteeing detection of all odd-count flips.

questions.questionText: In a (7, 4) Hamming code, how many data bits and parity (check) bits are present in each codeword?
questions.explanation: Total length n = 7, message bits k = 4, and parity check bits r = n - k = 3.

questions.questionText: What mathematical inequality determines the required number of parity bits 'r' for 'm' data bits in Hamming code?
questions.explanation: Hamming rule: 2^r must provide enough distinct bit combinations to point to each bit position or indicate no error: 2^r >= m + r + 1.

questions.questionText: Why is CRC widely used in hardware data links (Ethernet, Wi-Fi) over simple checksums?
questions.explanation: CRC polynomials detect burst errors up to r bits with 100% certainty and are implemented in linear feedback shift registers.

options.optionText: It detects burst errors of length up to polynomial degree with high probability using simple shift-register hardware

questions.questionText: What is the maximum theoretical channel throughput of Pure ALOHA?
questions.explanation: Pure ALOHA has a vulnerable period of 2 * T_frame, yielding maximum throughput S = G * e^(-2G) = 1/(2e) approx 18.4% at G=0.5.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum theoretical channel throughput of Slotted ALOHA?
questions.explanation: By restricting transmissions to discrete time slot boundaries, vulnerable time is halved, doubling throughput to 1/e approx 36.8%.

questions.questionText: In CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), what does a station do upon detecting a collision?
questions.explanation: The transmitting station immediately halts transmission and sends a jam signal to ensure all nodes register the collision.

options.optionText: Stops transmitting data immediately and broadcasts a 32-bit jam signal across the wire

questions.questionText: What algorithm is used in CSMA/CD to determine how long a station should wait before retransmitting after a collision?
questions.explanation: After collision 'k', stations wait a random number of slot times between 0 and 2^(min(k, 10)) - 1.

questions.questionText: In an Ethernet network, what is the fundamental relationship between minimum frame size, bandwidth, and propagation delay?
questions.explanation: To guarantee a sender detects collisions before completing transmission, T_frame >= 2 * T_prop.

options.optionText: Transmission time (Tt) must be greater than or equal to twice the round-trip propagation delay (2 * Tp)
Tt must be equal to Tp

questions.questionText: What is the standard minimum frame size for IEEE 802.3 10 Mbps Ethernet?
questions.explanation: 64 bytes is the standard minimum Ethernet frame size, ensuring collision detection across maximum cable segments.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum payload size (MTU) of a standard Ethernet frame?
questions.explanation: Standard Ethernet frames carry a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 1500 bytes of IP payload.

questions.questionText: Why is CSMA/CA (Collision Avoidance) used in Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) instead of CSMA/CD?
questions.explanation: Wireless transmission energy dwarfs received signal energy, blinding the radio from detecting concurrent collisions while transmitting.

options.optionText: Wireless transceivers cannot transmit and listen concurrently on the same channel to detect collisions

questions.questionText: Which handshaking mechanism in CSMA/CA solves the 'Hidden Terminal Problem' in wireless networks?
questions.explanation: RTS/CTS frames reserve channel access and alert hidden nodes via the Network Allocation Vector (NAV).

options.optionText: RTS (Request to Send) and CTS (Clear to Send)

questions.questionText: Which IEEE standard specifies Token Ring networks?
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.5 specifies Token Ring; 802.3 is Ethernet, 802.11 is Wi-Fi, and 802.15 is Bluetooth/Zigbee.

questions.questionText: What is the total bit length of an IPv4 address?
questions.explanation: IPv4 addresses consist of 32 bits organized as 4 decimal octets separated by dots (e.g., 192.168.1.1).

questions.questionText: What is the first octet range for Class A IPv4 addresses in classful addressing?
questions.explanation: Class A addresses begin with leading bit '0' and span first octet values 1 to 126 (127 is reserved for loopback).

questions.questionText: What is the default subnet mask for a Class B IPv4 network?
questions.explanation: Class B reserves 16 bits for Network ID and 16 bits for Host ID: default mask 255.255.0.0.

questions.questionText: Which IPv4 address class is specifically reserved for Multicast transmission?
questions.explanation: Class D addresses (prefix 1110, range 224-239) are designated for one-to-many multicast groups.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the IPv4 loopback address 127.0.0.1 (localhost)?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 loops packets back within the local OS kernel to test network software functionality.

options.optionText: To test the local TCP/IP protocol stack and internal inter-process communication without sending packets to the wire
To broadcast to all LAN devices

questions.questionText: What is the size of an IPv6 address in bits?
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses represented as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits separated by colons.

questions.questionText: Which protocol resolves a known logical IP address to a physical MAC address on a local network?
questions.explanation: ARP broadcasts an 'ARP Request' on the local LAN to discover the hardware MAC address matching a destination IP.

questions.questionText: Which protocol allows diskless workstations to obtain their IP address from a server upon booting?
questions.explanation: RARP queries a centralized server to retrieve the IP address corresponding to a known physical MAC address.

questions.questionText: What protocol is used by network diagnostic tools like `ping` and `traceroute` to report errors and echo packets?
questions.explanation: ICMP carries operational status messages, Echo Request/Reply (ping), and Time Exceeded (traceroute) notifications.

questions.questionText: What is the primary role of NAT (Network Address Translation) in modern IP networking?
questions.explanation: NAT conserves IPv4 addresses by translating private RFC 1918 addresses into shared public IPs at the border router.

options.optionText: Maps multiple private non-routable IP addresses to one or more globally routable public IP addresses

questions.questionText: Dijkstra's shortest path routing algorithm is categorized as which type of routing algorithm?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra computes shortest paths on a globally synchronized topological link-state database (used in OSPF).

questions.questionText: Distance Vector routing protocols (such as RIP) rely on which mathematical algorithm?
questions.explanation: Distance vector routing iteratively updates neighbour vectors using Bellman-Ford equation: D_x(y) = min_v { c(x,v) + D_v(y) }.

questions.questionText: What severe routing pathology occurs in Distance Vector protocols when a link fails, causing routers to slowly increment hop counts?
questions.explanation: Count-to-infinity occurs when two or more routers propagate stale metrics after link failure, slowly counting up to infinity.

questions.questionText: Which technique helps mitigate the Count-to-Infinity problem by preventing a router from advertising a route back out the interface it learned it from?
questions.explanation: Split Horizon dictates that route information is never broadcast back to the node from which it was received.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum hop count allowed by the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) before a destination is declared unreachable?
questions.explanation: RIP limits path length to 15 hops; 16 hops signifies an unreachable network.

questions.questionText: Which Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) is an open-standard Link-State protocol that organizes networks into hierarchical Areas?
questions.explanation: OSPF uses link-state advertisements, Dijkstra calculations, and hierarchical Area 0 (Backbone Area).

questions.questionText: Which exterior routing protocol is the standard inter-autonomous system (AS) routing protocol of the global Internet?
questions.explanation: BGP-4 is a path-vector exterior gateway protocol that interconnects distinct Autonomous Systems across the Internet.

questions.questionText: In traffic shaping, which algorithm transmits packets at an absolutely constant, smooth output rate regardless of burstiness?
questions.explanation: A Leaky Bucket drains packets at an invariant, fixed rate, smoothing out bursts completely.

questions.questionText: How does a Token Bucket traffic shaper differ from a Leaky Bucket shaper?
questions.explanation: Token buckets permit bursts of traffic when sufficient tokens have accumulated in the bucket.

options.optionText: It allows regulated bursty traffic transmissions up to the accumulated token limit

questions.questionText: What happens in TCP when a router drops a packet due to internal buffer queue exhaustion?
questions.explanation: TCP treats packet loss as an implicit signal of network congestion and reduces its transmission rate (AIMD).

options.optionText: Sender infers network congestion upon timeout or 3 duplicate ACKs and throttles its congestion window

questions.questionText: What are the core differences between TCP and UDP?
questions.explanation: TCP guarantees in-order, error-free delivery via acknowledgments; UDP is lightweight with minimal header overhead and no guarantees.

options.optionText: TCP is connectionless and unreliable; UDP is connection-oriented
TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, and byte-stream; UDP is connectionless, unreliable, and datagram-oriented

questions.questionText: How many packets are exchanged in a standard TCP Connection Establishment Handshake?
questions.explanation: The 3-way handshake synchronizes sequence numbers: Client sends SYN, Server replies SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK.

questions.questionText: How many segments are typically exchanged to gracefully close a TCP connection?
questions.explanation: TCP connection teardown uses a 4-way handshake: each half of the full-duplex link is closed independently with FIN/ACK.

questions.questionText: In TCP congestion control, what algorithm exponentially doubles the congestion window (cwnd) every Round Trip Time (RTT)?
questions.explanation: Slow Start begins with cwnd = 1 MSS and increments cwnd by 1 for each received ACK, effectively doubling cwnd each RTT.

questions.questionText: What is the standard port number for the HTTP web protocol?
questions.explanation: HTTP operates on well-known TCP port 80; HTTPS operates on encrypted port 443.

questions.questionText: What is the standard port number for DNS (Domain Name System) queries?
questions.explanation: DNS uses port 53 over UDP for lightweight queries and over TCP for large zone transfers.

questions.questionText: What is the standard port number used by SMTP to send outbound emails between mail servers?
questions.explanation: SMTP runs over TCP port 25 for inter-server mail transfer (client submission uses 587).

questions.questionText: Which transport protocol is preferred for real-time applications like VoIP, online gaming, and live video streaming?
questions.explanation: UDP avoids head-of-line blocking and retransmission delays, making it ideal for low-latency real-time media.

questions.questionText: What is the primary role of the Domain Name System (DNS)?
questions.explanation: DNS serves as the phonebook of the Internet, mapping hostname strings to 32-bit/128-bit IP addresses.

options.optionText: Assigns IP addresses dynamically to LAN clients
Translates human-readable domain names (e.g. example.com) into machine-routable IP addresses

questions.questionText: Which protocol is used by email clients to retrieve messages from a mail server while keeping emails synchronized on the server across multiple devices?
questions.explanation: IMAP synchronizes mailbox state across clients; POP3 typically downloads and deletes emails locally.

questions.questionText: In Symmetric-Key Cryptography (e.g. AES, DES):
questions.explanation: Symmetric cryptography uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption operations.

options.optionText: Two different keys are used for encryption and decryption
The identical secret key is shared and used for both encryption and decryption

questions.questionText: In Asymmetric (Public-Key) Cryptography (e.g. RSA):
questions.explanation: Public key encryption allows anyone to encrypt messages, but only the holder of the matching private key can decrypt them.

options.optionText: Data encrypted with the recipient's Public Key can only be decrypted with that recipient's Private Key
No mathematical relationship exists between keys

questions.questionText: How does a Digital Signature ensure authenticity and non-repudiation in electronic messages?
questions.explanation: Encrypting a message hash with one's private key proves origin authenticity and ensures the sender cannot deny sending it.

options.optionText: Sender encrypts the message with recipient's public key
Sender encrypts the cryptographic hash of the message with the sender's Private Key

questions.questionText: What is the primary function of a Network Firewall?
questions.explanation: A firewall enforces security perimeter policies, permitting or blocking traffic flows based on IP, port, or packet inspection.

options.optionText: Monitor, filter, and control incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between a Packet-Filtering Firewall and a Stateful Inspection Firewall?
questions.explanation: Stateful firewalls track TCP handshakes, sequence numbers, and connection states to prevent spoofing attacks.

options.optionText: Packet filtering is faster but inspects packets in isolation without connection state; Stateful firewall tracks TCP connection state and context
Stateful firewall cannot filter IP addresses
Packet filtering operates at Application layer

testsWithQuestions.title: BCA-504 Numerical: 100 Questions Complete Subject Exam
testsWithQuestions.description: Comprehensive 100-question exam covering absolute/relative errors, Bisection, Regula Falsi, Newton-Raphson, Gauss Elimination & Seidel, finite difference operators, Newton/Lagrange interpolation, Simpson's rules, and RK4.

questions.questionText: If X is the true value and X' is the approximate value, what is the mathematical formula for Absolute Error (E_a)?
questions.explanation: Absolute Error is the absolute magnitude of difference between true and approximate values: E_a = |X - X'|.

questions.questionText: What is the definition of Relative Error (E_r)?
questions.explanation: Relative Error normalizes absolute error by the true value: E_r = |X - X'| / |X|.

options.optionText: Absolute Error divided by True Value (|X - X'| / |X|)
True Value divided by Absolute Error

questions.questionText: How is Percentage Error (E_p) computed from Relative Error (E_r)?
questions.explanation: Percentage Error is the relative error expressed as a percentage: E_p = E_r * 100%.

questions.questionText: Rounding off the number 3.14159265 to four decimal places yields:
questions.explanation: The 5th decimal digit is 9 (>= 5), so the 4th digit 5 is incremented by 1 giving 3.1416.

questions.questionText: Truncation error in numerical computation is introduced primarily by:
questions.explanation: Truncation error arises when infinite processes (e.g. Taylor series) are truncated to finite steps.

options.optionText: Replacing an infinite mathematical series with a finite number of terms

questions.questionText: How many significant digits are present in the measurement 0.005040?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: '5040' has 4 significant digits.

questions.questionText: If an approximate number is correct to 'n' decimal places, the maximum absolute error does not exceed:
questions.explanation: When rounded to n decimal places, the absolute error is bounded by half a unit in the last place: <= 0.5 * 10^(-n).

questions.questionText: What is the absolute error when 2/3 is approximated as 0.667?
questions.explanation: True value = 0.6666667..., Approx = 0.667. Absolute error = |0.6666667 - 0.667| approx 0.000333.

questions.questionText: Which error is inherently present before any computation begins, due to physical measurement limitations?
questions.explanation: Inherent errors arise from measurement uncertainties, experimental tolerances, or simplified initial modeling.

questions.questionText: Propagation of error in addition: if X = A + B, the maximum absolute error in X is bounded by:
questions.explanation: In addition and subtraction, absolute errors add directly: Delta X <= Delta A + Delta B.

questions.questionText: The Bisection method for finding roots of f(x) = 0 is based on which fundamental calculus theorem?
questions.explanation: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b] and f(a)*f(b) < 0, Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one root in (a, b).

questions.questionText: What is the rate / order of convergence of the Bisection Method?
questions.explanation: The interval of uncertainty is halved at each step, giving linear convergence with rate 1/2.

questions.questionText: How many iterations of Bisection method are required to achieve an error tolerance epsilon for initial interval [a, b]?
questions.explanation: Since error after n steps is (b - a)/2^n <= epsilon, taking base-2 logarithms yields n >= log2((b - a) / epsilon).

questions.questionText: In Regula Falsi (Method of False Position), the next approximation root 'c' is given by the formula:
questions.explanation: Regula Falsi connects (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) with a secant chord, finding the x-intercept c = (a*f(b) - b*f(a))/(f(b) - f(a)).

questions.questionText: What is the order of convergence of the Newton-Raphson Method?
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson exhibits quadratic convergence (order 2) near simple roots: error satisfies e_(n+1) approx C * e_n^2.

questions.questionText: What is the recurrence relation for the Newton-Raphson iterative method?
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson linearizes f(x) using the tangent line: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n).

questions.questionText: Under which specific condition does the Newton-Raphson method fail completely (division by zero)?
questions.explanation: If the first derivative f'(x_n) is zero, the tangent line is horizontal and never intersects the x-axis.

questions.questionText: What is the iterative formula to compute the square root of a positive number 'N' using Newton-Raphson?
questions.explanation: For f(x) = x^2 - N = 0, f'(x) = 2x. Newton-Raphson yields x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - N)/(2x_n) = 0.5*(x_n + N/x_n).

questions.questionText: What is the order of convergence of the Secant Method?
questions.explanation: The Secant method approximates the derivative with a finite difference chord, converging superlinearly at order (1 + sqrt(5))/2 approx 1.618.

questions.questionText: How many function evaluations per iteration are required by the Secant Method once initialized?
questions.explanation: The Secant method retains the previous f(x_(n-1)) and evaluates only f(x_n) at each step.

questions.questionText: In Fixed-Point Iteration x = g(x), what is the sufficient condition for convergence in an interval containing root alpha?
questions.explanation: By the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem, |g'(x)| <= k < 1 guarantees unique contraction mapping and convergence.

options.optionText: |g'(x)| < 1 for all x in the interval

questions.questionText: Which root-finding method is guaranteed to always converge if an initial bracket [a, b] with f(a)*f(b) < 0 is given?
questions.explanation: Bisection is unconditionally guaranteed to bracket and converge to a root for continuous functions.

questions.questionText: Newton-Raphson method applied to find the reciprocal of 'N' (1/N) yields the division-free iterative formula:
If an algebraic equation has a multiple root of multiplicity m > 1, how is Newton-Raphson modified to maintain quadratic convergence?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the correction term by multiplicity m restores quadratic convergence: x_(n+1) = x_n - m*(f(x_n)/f'(x_n)).

questions.questionText: The iteration x_(n+1) = 0.5 * (x_n + 2/x_n) converges to:
questions.explanation: Setting x = 0.5*(x + 2/x) yields 2x = x + 2/x => x^2 = 2 => x = sqrt(2).

questions.questionText: In Gauss Elimination method, the augmented matrix [A | B] is transformed into which form?
questions.explanation: Gauss elimination uses forward elimination to reduce the matrix to upper triangular form, solved by back substitution.

questions.questionText: How does the Gauss-Jordan method differ from standard Gauss Elimination?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Jordan eliminates both above and below the pivot, reducing [A | I] to [I | A^(-1)] or [A | B] to [I | X].

options.optionText: It transforms the coefficient matrix directly into an Identity / Diagonal matrix, eliminating the need for back substitution
It does not use row operations

questions.questionText: What is the computational complexity (number of arithmetic operations) of Gauss Elimination for an n x n system?
questions.explanation: Gauss elimination requires approximately 2n^3 / 3 floating point multiplications and additions.

questions.questionText: Why is Partial Pivoting (row interchanges) employed during Gauss Elimination?
questions.explanation: Partial pivoting places the largest element in column k on the diagonal, bounding multiplier magnitudes <= 1.

options.optionText: To avoid division by zero and minimize round-off errors by choosing the largest available pivot element in magnitude

questions.questionText: In LU Decomposition (Doolittle method), the coefficient matrix A is factored as A = L * U, where L has:
questions.explanation: Doolittle's algorithm fixes diagonal entries l_ii = 1; Crout's algorithm fixes u_ii = 1.

options.optionText: Ones on the main diagonal (Unit Lower Triangular)

questions.questionText: Cholesky Decomposition A = L * L^T is applicable if and only if the matrix A is:
questions.explanation: Cholesky factorization requires A to be strictly symmetric (A = A^T) and positive definite (x^T A x > 0 for all x != 0).

questions.questionText: What is the sufficient condition for convergence of iterative methods (Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel)?
questions.explanation: Strict diagonal dominance guarantees that the spectral radius of the iteration matrix is strictly less than 1.

options.optionText: The coefficient matrix must be Strictly Diagonally Dominant (|a_ii| > sum_{j != i} |a_ij|)

questions.questionText: How does the Gauss-Seidel method differ fundamentally from the Gauss-Jacobi method?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Seidel immediately incorporates updated x_i values in subsequent equations, converging roughly twice as fast as Jacobi.

options.optionText: Gauss-Seidel uses the newly computed values of unknowns immediately within the same iteration cycle
Gauss-Seidel only updates at the very end of all equations

questions.questionText: A system of linear equations is called 'Ill-Conditioned' when:
questions.explanation: Ill-conditioned systems have very large condition numbers (||A|| * ||A^(-1)|| >> 1), causing extreme sensitivity to rounding.

options.optionText: A tiny change in coefficients or constants causes a drastic, disproportionate change in the solution vector
It has more equations than unknowns

questions.questionText: The Condition Number of a matrix A is defined as:
questions.explanation: Condition number kappa(A) = ||A|| * ||A^(-1)|| measures sensitivity; kappa(A) = 1 is ideal.

questions.questionText: In the Gauss-Seidel method for 3 equations, how many iterations does it typically take relative to Gauss-Jacobi?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Seidel generally converges about twice as fast because spectral radius of Seidel iteration matrix is approx (spectral radius of Jacobi)^2.

options.optionText: Approximately half as many iterations (converges twice as fast)

questions.questionText: What happens to an iterative linear solver if the coefficient matrix is NOT diagonally dominant?
questions.explanation: Strict diagonal dominance is sufficient but not necessary; convergence holds whenever spectral radius < 1.

options.optionText: May still converge if spectral radius rho(H) < 1, but diagonal dominance is the standard sufficient guarantee

questions.questionText: Relaxation methods (SOR - Successive Over-Relaxation) introduce a parameter omega. For over-relaxation to accelerate convergence, omega must satisfy:
questions.explanation: SOR with 1 < omega < 2 accelerates convergence; 0 < omega < 1 is under-relaxation used for divergent systems.

questions.questionText: Which matrix norm is defined as the maximum absolute row sum: max_i sum_j |a_ij|?
questions.explanation: The infinity norm is the maximum row sum; the 1-norm is the maximum column sum.

questions.questionText: If det(A) = 0 for coefficient matrix A in A*X = B, the system has:
questions.explanation: A singular matrix det(A)=0 indicates linearly dependent rows, resulting in either infinite solutions or inconsistency.

options.optionText: Either no solution (inconsistent) or infinitely many solutions

questions.questionText: The Forward Difference Operator Delta operating on y_0 is defined as:
questions.explanation: The forward difference Delta y_i = y_(i+1) - y_i.

questions.questionText: The Backward Difference Operator Nabla operating on y_1 is defined as:
questions.explanation: The backward difference Nabla y_i = y_i - y_(i-1).

questions.questionText: The Shift Operator E operating on y_i produces:
questions.explanation: The shift operator shifts the argument by one interval step h: E y_i = y_(i+1).

questions.questionText: What is the algebraic relationship between the Shift operator E and Forward Difference operator Delta?
questions.explanation: Since E y = y(x + h) = y(x) + Delta y(x) = (1 + Delta) y, we have E = 1 + Delta.

questions.questionText: What is the algebraic relationship between the Shift operator E and Backward Difference operator Nabla?
questions.explanation: Nabla y_i = y_i - y_(i-1) = (1 - E^(-1)) y_i, so Nabla = 1 - E^(-1).

questions.questionText: The Central Difference Operator delta operating on y_i is defined as:
questions.explanation: The central difference delta y_i = y_(i + 1/2) - y_(i - 1/2) = (E^(1/2) - E^(-1/2)) y_i.

questions.questionText: The Averaging Operator mu is defined as:
What is the n-th forward difference Delta^n of a polynomial of degree n: P_n(x) = a_n * x^n + ...?
questions.explanation: The n-th difference of an n-th degree polynomial is constant: Delta^n P_n(x) = n! * a_n * h^n.

questions.questionText: What is the (n + 1)-th forward difference Delta^(n + 1) of a polynomial of degree n?
questions.explanation: Since the n-th difference of a degree-n polynomial is constant, all subsequent differences are zero: Delta^(n+1) P_n(x) = 0.

questions.questionText: What is the value of Delta (c) where 'c' is an invariant constant?
questions.explanation: For constant c, Delta c = c - c = 0.

questions.questionText: Evaluate Delta (x^2) with step length h = 1:
What is the fundamental operator relation connecting Shift operator E, interval h, and differential operator D = d/dx?
questions.explanation: By Taylor expansion: E f(x) = f(x + h) = sum (hD)^n / n! f(x) = e^(hD) f(x). Hence E = e^(hD).

questions.questionText: The factorial polynomial x^(3) (x to the 3rd factorial power) with step h = 1 is defined as:
questions.explanation: Factorial notation: x^(n) = x(x - 1)(x - 2)...(x - n + 1). For n=3: x(x - 1)(x - 2).

questions.questionText: What is the first difference Delta [x^(n)] of a factorial polynomial with step h = 1?
questions.explanation: Factorial polynomials mirror standard differentiation under differences: Delta x^(n) = n * x^(n - 1).

questions.questionText: The relation between central difference operator delta and shift operator E is:
Newton's Forward Interpolation Formula is best suited for interpolating values of y at x located:
questions.explanation: Newton's Forward formula utilizes forward differences from the top, ideal near x_0.

options.optionText: Near the end of a tabulated set of values
Near the beginning of a tabulated set of values
Near the center of the table

questions.questionText: Newton's Backward Interpolation Formula is primarily employed when the target value of x is:
questions.explanation: Newton's Backward formula begins at the base x_n and propagates upward via backward differences Nabla.

options.optionText: Near the beginning of the table
Near the end of the tabulated values

questions.questionText: What parameter 'u' (or 'p') is used in Newton's Forward Interpolation formula?
questions.explanation: In Newton's forward formula, the normalized step variable is u = (x - x_0)/h.

questions.questionText: What parameter 'v' (or 'p') is used in Newton's Backward Interpolation formula?
questions.explanation: In Newton's backward formula, the variable is measured from the end: v = (x - x_n)/h.

questions.questionText: Which central difference interpolation formula uses the arithmetic mean of Gauss Forward and Gauss Backward formulas?
questions.explanation: Stirling's formula is the arithmetic average of Gauss forward and Gauss backward interpolation formulas.

questions.questionText: Which central difference formula involves ONLY even differences and is widely used for astronomy tables?
questions.explanation: Everett's formula expresses interpolation solely in terms of function values and even backward/central differences.

questions.questionText: Stirling's central difference interpolation formula produces optimal accuracy when |u| satisfies:
questions.explanation: Stirling's formula gives best accuracy near the center where -0.25 <= u <= 0.25 (Bessel is preferred for 0.25 <= u <= 0.75).

questions.questionText: Lagrange's Interpolation Formula is applicable for:
questions.explanation: Lagrange interpolation does not require equal step spacing h; it handles arbitrary distinct abscissas.

options.optionText: Both equally and unequally spaced intervals of argument x

questions.questionText: In Lagrange's interpolation formula with n+1 points, each Lagrange coefficient polynomial L_i(x) satisfies:
questions.explanation: Lagrange cardinal polynomials satisfy the cardinal property L_i(x_j) = delta_ij.

options.optionText: L_i(x_j) = 1 if i = j, and 0 if i != j (Kronecker delta)

questions.questionText: What is the degree of the unique interpolating polynomial fitting (n + 1) distinct data points?
questions.explanation: By the polynomial interpolation uniqueness theorem, exactly one polynomial of degree at most n passes through n+1 points.

questions.questionText: The first divided difference of f(x) over distinct points x_0 and x_1 is denoted and defined as:
questions.explanation: The first divided difference is the slope of the secant chord: f[x_0, x_1] = (f(x_1) - f(x_0))/(x_1 - x_0).

questions.questionText: Divided differences possess which important mathematical symmetry property?
questions.explanation: Divided differences are symmetric: f[x_0, x_1] = f[x_1, x_0], and f[x_0, x_1, x_2] is invariant to any rearrangement of arguments.

options.optionText: They change sign when arguments are swapped
They are completely symmetric functions of their arguments (invariant to permutations)
They depend on order of points

questions.questionText: If two arguments in a divided difference coincide, f[x_0, x_0] equals:
questions.explanation: By taking the limit as x_1 -> x_0, f[x_0, x_1] becomes lim (f(x_1) - f(x_0))/(x_1 - x_0) = f'(x_0).

questions.questionText: What is the n-th divided difference of a polynomial of degree n?
questions.explanation: The n-th divided difference of an n-th degree polynomial P(x) = a_n * x^n + ... is constant and equals a_n.

questions.questionText: What is the (n + 1)-th divided difference of a polynomial of degree n?
questions.explanation: All divided differences of order higher than the degree of the polynomial are identically zero.

questions.questionText: What is the main practical drawback of Lagrange's interpolation formula compared to Newton's Divided Difference form?
questions.explanation: Newton's divided difference form is incremental: adding a point simply appends one new term without invalidating previous terms.

options.optionText: Adding a new data point requires recomputing all Lagrange basis terms from scratch

questions.questionText: Inverse Interpolation is the process of:
questions.explanation: Inverse interpolation solves for x given y = f(x), using Lagrange's formula treating x as a function of y.

options.optionText: Finding the value of the independent variable x corresponding to a given y

questions.questionText: Hermite's Interpolation formula matches:
questions.explanation: Hermite interpolation fits a polynomial matching both y(x_i) and y'(x_i), yielding degree 2n+1 for n+1 nodes.

options.optionText: Both function values y_i AND first derivative values y'_i at every node

questions.questionText: Cubic Spline interpolation fits piecewise cubic polynomials between adjacent points with continuous:
questions.explanation: A cubic spline S(x) guarantees continuity of S(x), S'(x), and S''(x) across all knot points, avoiding Runge phenomenon oscillations.

options.optionText: First and second derivatives at all interior knots
