options.optionText: Cannot be directly instantiated with the `new` operator

questions.questionText: Can an abstract class define a constructor?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes have constructors to initialize their own fields when subclasses call `super()`.

options.optionText: No, abstract classes cannot have constructors
Yes, invoked via super() by subclasses during subclass instantiation
Only if the constructor is private

questions.questionText: Which keyword is used by a class to implement one or more interfaces?
questions.explanation: The `implements` keyword binds a class to one or more interface contracts: `class A implements B, C`.

questions.questionText: In Java 8 and later, interfaces can contain concrete method implementations using which modifier?
questions.explanation: Java 8 introduced `default` and `static` methods inside interfaces to allow backward-compatible API evolution.

questions.questionText: What are the implicit modifiers for all variables declared inside a Java Interface?
questions.explanation: All fields declared in an interface are implicitly `public static final` (constants).

questions.questionText: What are the implicit modifiers for abstract methods declared inside an interface?
questions.explanation: Interface methods without a body are implicitly `public abstract`.

questions.questionText: Which access modifier restricts the visibility of a class member exclusively to its enclosing class?
questions.explanation: The `private` modifier restricts visibility solely to the declaring class.

testsWithQuestions.title: Computer Networks (BCA-503) Semester Mock Paper
testsWithQuestions.description: 50-question mock test covering OSI/TCP-IP models, sliding window, routing, and IP addressing.

questions.questionText: Which network topology connects every computer to a central device such as a hub or switch?
questions.explanation: In Star topology, every node connects via dedicated point-to-point links to a central hub/switch.

questions.questionText: In a Fully Connected Mesh topology having 'n' devices, how many physical duplex links are required?
questions.explanation: A full mesh network requires n(n - 1) / 2 physical bidirectional links to connect all node pairs.

questions.questionText: Which physical transmission medium uses light pulses to transmit data at very high speeds with zero EMI?
questions.explanation: Fiber optic cables carry data as pulses of light guided through silica glass fibers, unaffected by electromagnetic interference.

questions.questionText: What physical phenomenon governs the transmission of light pulses inside an optical fiber core?
questions.explanation: Total Internal Reflection occurs when light strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle.

questions.questionText: Which type of switching dedicates a physical communication path between sender and receiver for the entire session?
questions.explanation: Circuit switching (used in traditional telephony) reserves dedicated end-to-end bandwidth before data flows.

questions.questionText: What is the primary advantage of Packet Switching over Circuit Switching?
questions.explanation: Packet switching dynamically shares bandwidth among active nodes, utilizing transmission capacity far more efficiently.

options.optionText: Dynamic statistical multiplexing and high link utilization efficiency

questions.questionText: Which network category covers a small geographical area such as a single room, lab, or office building?
questions.explanation: LANs operate across bounded geographic areas (homes, offices) typically spanning less than a few kilometers.

questions.questionText: In a Bus topology, what critical component must be placed at both ends of the backbone coaxial cable to absorb reflections?
questions.explanation: Terminators match impedance at the cable extremities, absorbing signals to eliminate signal bounce/reflection.

questions.questionText: Attenuation in computer networking refers to:
questions.explanation: Attenuation is the gradual decay of signal amplitude over transmission distance, compensated by amplifiers/repeaters.

options.optionText: Loss of signal strength and energy as a wave propagates over physical distance
Packet loss due to buffer overflow

questions.questionText: What is the theoretical maximum channel capacity of a noiseless channel according to Nyquist theorem?
questions.explanation: Nyquist formula C = 2B log2(M) gives maximum bit rate for bandwidth B and discrete signal levels M in noiseless media.

questions.questionText: What does Shannon's Channel Capacity theorem define for a noisy channel?
questions.explanation: Shannon's capacity formula establishes the upper transmission bound in the presence of Gaussian thermal noise.

options.optionText: Theoretical maximum error-free data rate: C = B log2(1 + SNR)

questions.questionText: Which unguided (wireless) transmission band is used for television remotes and short-range line-of-sight devices?
questions.explanation: Infrared signals cannot penetrate solid walls and are used for secure, short-range indoor devices and remotes.

questions.questionText: Which transmission impairment is caused by the unwanted electrical coupling between adjacent wire pairs in a cable?
questions.explanation: Crosstalk happens when electromagnetic radiation from one twisted pair leaks into an adjacent wire pair.

questions.questionText: A communication mode where transmission can occur in both directions simultaneously is called:
questions.explanation: Full-Duplex (e.g., standard telephone or switched Ethernet) supports concurrent bidirectional transmission.

questions.questionText: A walkie-talkie where users take turns transmitting one at a time is an example of:
questions.explanation: Half-Duplex allows bidirectional communication, but only one party may transmit on the shared frequency at a given moment.

questions.questionText: How many layers are specified in the standard ISO-OSI Reference Model?
questions.explanation: The OSI model specifies 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Data Link Layer?
questions.explanation: Data Link PDU is a Frame; Physical is Bit; Network is Packet; Transport is Segment.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Network Layer?
questions.explanation: The Network layer encapsulates transport segments into Packets / Datagrams with logical IP addresses.

questions.questionText: What is the Protocol Data Unit (PDU) called at the Transport Layer?
questions.explanation: The Transport layer encapsulates application messages into Segments (TCP) or User Datagrams (UDP).

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer is responsible for end-to-end process-to-process delivery, flow control, and port addressing?
questions.explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides process-to-process communication using source and destination port numbers.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer performs cryptographic encryption/decryption, data compression, and character set translation?
questions.explanation: The Presentation layer (Layer 6) handles abstract data formatting, encoding (ASCII/Unicode), and SSL/TLS encryption.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates dialog sessions between cooperating applications?
questions.explanation: The Session layer (Layer 5) maintains session tokens, dialog control (simplex/half/full duplex), and synchronization checkpoints.

questions.questionText: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets across interconnected disparate networks using logical addresses?
questions.explanation: The Network layer determines optimal paths across hops using IP routing protocols.

questions.questionText: How many layers are defined in the original TCP/IP protocol suite?
questions.explanation: TCP/IP architecture defines 4 primary layers: Network Interface, Internet, Transport, and Application.

questions.questionText: Which device operates at the Physical layer (Layer 1) to regenerate and retransmit degraded electrical signals?
questions.explanation: Repeaters and hubs operate at Layer 1, regenerating electrical bit streams without inspecting headers.

questions.questionText: A standard Layer 2 Network Switch makes packet forwarding decisions based on:
questions.explanation: Layer 2 switches maintain MAC Address Tables (CAM tables) to forward frames to specific physical ports.

questions.questionText: A Network Router operates at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network Layer) and inspect IP headers to make path routing decisions.

questions.questionText: Which network device connects two distinct network architectures operating on completely different protocol suites?
questions.explanation: A Gateway translates protocols across all 7 OSI layers, bridging incompatible networks.

questions.questionText: What is the size of an IEEE 802 standard MAC (Ethernet) address?
questions.explanation: Ethernet MAC addresses are 48-bit hardware identifiers represented as 12 hexadecimal digits (e.g., 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E).

questions.questionText: What are the first 3 bytes (24 bits) of an Ethernet MAC address known as?
questions.explanation: The first 24 bits are the IEEE-assigned OUI identifying the hardware manufacturer / vendor.

questions.questionText: In HDLC framing, what specific bit pattern is used as the start and end flag sequence?
questions.explanation: HDLC flags use 01111110 (six consecutive ones bounded by zeroes) to delimit frame boundaries.

questions.questionText: What technique does HDLC use to prevent the flag pattern (01111110) from accidentally appearing in payload data?
questions.explanation: Bit stuffing automatically inserts a '0' bit after any sequence of five consecutive '1' bits in the payload.

options.optionText: Bit Stuffing (inserting a 0 after five consecutive 1s)

questions.questionText: In Byte Stuffing (Character-Oriented Framing), which special escape character is stuffed before payload delimiter bytes?
questions.explanation: DLE (Data Link Escape) is stuffed before occurrences of DLE STX or DLE ETX inside data payload.

questions.questionText: What is 'Piggybacking' in data link layer protocols?
questions.explanation: Piggybacking appends acknowledgment numbers to outgoing reverse data frames, conserving bandwidth.

options.optionText: Delaying an acknowledgment (ACK) to attach it to the header of the next outgoing data frame
Compressing multiple packets into one frame

questions.questionText: In Stop-and-Wait ARQ, what happens if an acknowledgment (ACK) frame is lost in transit?
questions.explanation: Timeout expiration triggers retransmission of the unacknowledged frame.

options.optionText: The sender's retransmission timer expires and the data frame is automatically retransmitted

questions.questionText: In a Go-Back-N ARQ protocol with an m-bit sequence number, what is the maximum permissible sender window size?
questions.explanation: To avoid ambiguity between new frames and retransmissions, Go-Back-N sender window size must not exceed 2^m - 1.

questions.questionText: What is the receiver window size in Go-Back-N ARQ?
questions.explanation: Go-Back-N receivers accept frames strictly in sequence, maintaining a receive window size of 1 and discarding out-of-order frames.

questions.questionText: In Selective Repeat ARQ with an m-bit sequence number, what is the maximum sender and receiver window size?
questions.explanation: In Selective Repeat, both sender and receiver windows are equal, with maximum size 2^(m - 1) to prevent sequence overlap.

questions.questionText: Which ARQ flow control protocol retransmits ONLY the specific damaged or lost frame rather than subsequent frames?
questions.explanation: Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order frames and requests retransmission of only the specific missing sequence number.

questions.questionText: In HDLC, which frame type carries actual user data and piggybacked acknowledgment sequence numbers?
questions.explanation: I-Frames carry payload data along with N(S) send sequence and N(R) receive sequence acknowledgment numbers.

questions.questionText: In HDLC, Supervisory Frames (S-Frames) are primarily utilized for:
questions.explanation: S-Frames contain control commands for flow/error management without carrying payload data.

options.optionText: Flow control and error control (ACK, NAK, Receive Ready RR, Receive Not Ready RNR)

questions.questionText: In HDLC, Unnumbered Frames (U-Frames) are utilized for:
questions.explanation: U-Frames manage link initialization and teardown (e.g. Set Asynchronous Balanced Mode SABM).

options.optionText: Link setup, disconnect, mode setting (SABM, DISC), and reporting unrecoverable errors

questions.questionText: What is the efficiency of Stop-and-Wait protocol when propagation delay (Tp) is significantly larger than transmission time (Tt)?
questions.explanation: High latency satellite or long-haul links make Stop-and-Wait highly inefficient because sender idles waiting for ACKs.

options.optionText: Extremely low: Efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a) where a = Tp / Tt

questions.questionText: What does the parameter 'a' represent in data communication efficiency formulas?
questions.explanation: The parameter a = Tp / Tt measures how many packet lengths fill the pipe during round-trip propagation.

options.optionText: Ratio of propagation delay to transmission delay (Tp / Tt)

questions.questionText: Which data link layer protocol is universally used over direct point-to-point serial links and dial-up/DSL internet connections?
questions.explanation: PPP encapsulates packets over serial links and handles authentication (PAP/CHAP) and IP address negotiation.

questions.questionText: In Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), if the generator polynomial is of degree 'r', how many check bits (zeroes) are appended to the data bits before division?
questions.explanation: A generator polynomial of degree r requires appending exactly r zeroes to data before modulo-2 polynomial division.

questions.questionText: Modulo-2 arithmetic used in CRC calculations is mathematically equivalent to which bitwise operation?
questions.explanation: Modulo-2 addition and subtraction are identical and equivalent to the bitwise XOR operation without carries.

questions.questionText: To detect up to 'd' single-bit errors in any transmission, the minimum Hamming distance of the code must be:
questions.explanation: To detect d single-bit errors, the code words must have a minimum Hamming distance of d + 1.

questions.questionText: To correct up to 't' single-bit errors in any transmission, the minimum Hamming distance of the code must be:
questions.explanation: To guarantee correction of t errors, spheres of radius t around valid codewords must not overlap: d_min >= 2t + 1.

questions.questionText: What is the Hamming distance between the two codewords 1011101 and 1001001?
questions.explanation: Hamming distance is the count of differing bit positions: positions 3 and 5 differ, so distance is 2.

testsWithQuestions.title: Numerical Methods (BCA-504) Semester Mock Paper
testsWithQuestions.description: 50-question mock test covering Newton-Raphson, Gauss Elimination, finite differences, and RK4.

questions.questionText: If X is the true value and X' is the approximate value, what is the mathematical formula for Absolute Error (E_a)?
questions.explanation: Absolute Error is the absolute magnitude of difference between true and approximate values: E_a = |X - X'|.

questions.questionText: What is the definition of Relative Error (E_r)?
questions.explanation: Relative Error normalizes absolute error by the true value: E_r = |X - X'| / |X|.

options.optionText: Absolute Error divided by True Value (|X - X'| / |X|)
True Value divided by Absolute Error

questions.questionText: How is Percentage Error (E_p) computed from Relative Error (E_r)?
questions.explanation: Percentage Error is the relative error expressed as a percentage: E_p = E_r * 100%.

questions.questionText: Rounding off the number 3.14159265 to four decimal places yields:
questions.explanation: The 5th decimal digit is 9 (>= 5), so the 4th digit 5 is incremented by 1 giving 3.1416.

questions.questionText: Truncation error in numerical computation is introduced primarily by:
questions.explanation: Truncation error arises when infinite processes (e.g. Taylor series) are truncated to finite steps.

options.optionText: Replacing an infinite mathematical series with a finite number of terms

questions.questionText: How many significant digits are present in the measurement 0.005040?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant: '5040' has 4 significant digits.

questions.questionText: If an approximate number is correct to 'n' decimal places, the maximum absolute error does not exceed:
questions.explanation: When rounded to n decimal places, the absolute error is bounded by half a unit in the last place: <= 0.5 * 10^(-n).

questions.questionText: What is the absolute error when 2/3 is approximated as 0.667?
questions.explanation: True value = 0.6666667..., Approx = 0.667. Absolute error = |0.6666667 - 0.667| approx 0.000333.

questions.questionText: Which error is inherently present before any computation begins, due to physical measurement limitations?
questions.explanation: Inherent errors arise from measurement uncertainties, experimental tolerances, or simplified initial modeling.

questions.questionText: Propagation of error in addition: if X = A + B, the maximum absolute error in X is bounded by:
questions.explanation: In addition and subtraction, absolute errors add directly: Delta X <= Delta A + Delta B.

questions.questionText: The Bisection method for finding roots of f(x) = 0 is based on which fundamental calculus theorem?
questions.explanation: If f(x) is continuous on [a, b] and f(a)*f(b) < 0, Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees at least one root in (a, b).

questions.questionText: What is the rate / order of convergence of the Bisection Method?
questions.explanation: The interval of uncertainty is halved at each step, giving linear convergence with rate 1/2.

questions.questionText: How many iterations of Bisection method are required to achieve an error tolerance epsilon for initial interval [a, b]?
questions.explanation: Since error after n steps is (b - a)/2^n <= epsilon, taking base-2 logarithms yields n >= log2((b - a) / epsilon).

questions.questionText: In Regula Falsi (Method of False Position), the next approximation root 'c' is given by the formula:
questions.explanation: Regula Falsi connects (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)) with a secant chord, finding the x-intercept c = (a*f(b) - b*f(a))/(f(b) - f(a)).

questions.questionText: What is the order of convergence of the Newton-Raphson Method?
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson exhibits quadratic convergence (order 2) near simple roots: error satisfies e_(n+1) approx C * e_n^2.

questions.questionText: What is the recurrence relation for the Newton-Raphson iterative method?
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson linearizes f(x) using the tangent line: x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n).

questions.questionText: Under which specific condition does the Newton-Raphson method fail completely (division by zero)?
questions.explanation: If the first derivative f'(x_n) is zero, the tangent line is horizontal and never intersects the x-axis.

questions.questionText: What is the iterative formula to compute the square root of a positive number 'N' using Newton-Raphson?
questions.explanation: For f(x) = x^2 - N = 0, f'(x) = 2x. Newton-Raphson yields x_(n+1) = x_n - (x_n^2 - N)/(2x_n) = 0.5*(x_n + N/x_n).

questions.questionText: What is the order of convergence of the Secant Method?
questions.explanation: The Secant method approximates the derivative with a finite difference chord, converging superlinearly at order (1 + sqrt(5))/2 approx 1.618.

questions.questionText: How many function evaluations per iteration are required by the Secant Method once initialized?
questions.explanation: The Secant method retains the previous f(x_(n-1)) and evaluates only f(x_n) at each step.

questions.questionText: In Fixed-Point Iteration x = g(x), what is the sufficient condition for convergence in an interval containing root alpha?
questions.explanation: By the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem, |g'(x)| <= k < 1 guarantees unique contraction mapping and convergence.

options.optionText: |g'(x)| < 1 for all x in the interval

questions.questionText: Which root-finding method is guaranteed to always converge if an initial bracket [a, b] with f(a)*f(b) < 0 is given?
questions.explanation: Bisection is unconditionally guaranteed to bracket and converge to a root for continuous functions.

questions.questionText: Newton-Raphson method applied to find the reciprocal of 'N' (1/N) yields the division-free iterative formula:
If an algebraic equation has a multiple root of multiplicity m > 1, how is Newton-Raphson modified to maintain quadratic convergence?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the correction term by multiplicity m restores quadratic convergence: x_(n+1) = x_n - m*(f(x_n)/f'(x_n)).

questions.questionText: The iteration x_(n+1) = 0.5 * (x_n + 2/x_n) converges to:
questions.explanation: Setting x = 0.5*(x + 2/x) yields 2x = x + 2/x => x^2 = 2 => x = sqrt(2).

questions.questionText: In Gauss Elimination method, the augmented matrix [A | B] is transformed into which form?
questions.explanation: Gauss elimination uses forward elimination to reduce the matrix to upper triangular form, solved by back substitution.

questions.questionText: How does the Gauss-Jordan method differ from standard Gauss Elimination?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Jordan eliminates both above and below the pivot, reducing [A | I] to [I | A^(-1)] or [A | B] to [I | X].

options.optionText: It transforms the coefficient matrix directly into an Identity / Diagonal matrix, eliminating the need for back substitution
It does not use row operations

questions.questionText: What is the computational complexity (number of arithmetic operations) of Gauss Elimination for an n x n system?
questions.explanation: Gauss elimination requires approximately 2n^3 / 3 floating point multiplications and additions.

questions.questionText: Why is Partial Pivoting (row interchanges) employed during Gauss Elimination?
questions.explanation: Partial pivoting places the largest element in column k on the diagonal, bounding multiplier magnitudes <= 1.

options.optionText: To avoid division by zero and minimize round-off errors by choosing the largest available pivot element in magnitude

questions.questionText: In LU Decomposition (Doolittle method), the coefficient matrix A is factored as A = L * U, where L has:
questions.explanation: Doolittle's algorithm fixes diagonal entries l_ii = 1; Crout's algorithm fixes u_ii = 1.

options.optionText: Ones on the main diagonal (Unit Lower Triangular)

questions.questionText: Cholesky Decomposition A = L * L^T is applicable if and only if the matrix A is:
questions.explanation: Cholesky factorization requires A to be strictly symmetric (A = A^T) and positive definite (x^T A x > 0 for all x != 0).

questions.questionText: What is the sufficient condition for convergence of iterative methods (Gauss-Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel)?
questions.explanation: Strict diagonal dominance guarantees that the spectral radius of the iteration matrix is strictly less than 1.

options.optionText: The coefficient matrix must be Strictly Diagonally Dominant (|a_ii| > sum_{j != i} |a_ij|)

questions.questionText: How does the Gauss-Seidel method differ fundamentally from the Gauss-Jacobi method?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Seidel immediately incorporates updated x_i values in subsequent equations, converging roughly twice as fast as Jacobi.

options.optionText: Gauss-Seidel uses the newly computed values of unknowns immediately within the same iteration cycle
Gauss-Seidel only updates at the very end of all equations

questions.questionText: A system of linear equations is called 'Ill-Conditioned' when:
questions.explanation: Ill-conditioned systems have very large condition numbers (||A|| * ||A^(-1)|| >> 1), causing extreme sensitivity to rounding.

options.optionText: A tiny change in coefficients or constants causes a drastic, disproportionate change in the solution vector
It has more equations than unknowns

questions.questionText: The Condition Number of a matrix A is defined as:
questions.explanation: Condition number kappa(A) = ||A|| * ||A^(-1)|| measures sensitivity; kappa(A) = 1 is ideal.

questions.questionText: In the Gauss-Seidel method for 3 equations, how many iterations does it typically take relative to Gauss-Jacobi?
questions.explanation: Gauss-Seidel generally converges about twice as fast because spectral radius of Seidel iteration matrix is approx (spectral radius of Jacobi)^2.

options.optionText: Approximately half as many iterations (converges twice as fast)

questions.questionText: What happens to an iterative linear solver if the coefficient matrix is NOT diagonally dominant?
questions.explanation: Strict diagonal dominance is sufficient but not necessary; convergence holds whenever spectral radius < 1.

options.optionText: May still converge if spectral radius rho(H) < 1, but diagonal dominance is the standard sufficient guarantee

questions.questionText: Relaxation methods (SOR - Successive Over-Relaxation) introduce a parameter omega. For over-relaxation to accelerate convergence, omega must satisfy:
questions.explanation: SOR with 1 < omega < 2 accelerates convergence; 0 < omega < 1 is under-relaxation used for divergent systems.

questions.questionText: Which matrix norm is defined as the maximum absolute row sum: max_i sum_j |a_ij|?
questions.explanation: The infinity norm is the maximum row sum; the 1-norm is the maximum column sum.

questions.questionText: If det(A) = 0 for coefficient matrix A in A*X = B, the system has:
questions.explanation: A singular matrix det(A)=0 indicates linearly dependent rows, resulting in either infinite solutions or inconsistency.

options.optionText: Either no solution (inconsistent) or infinitely many solutions

questions.questionText: The Forward Difference Operator Delta operating on y_0 is defined as:
questions.explanation: The forward difference Delta y_i = y_(i+1) - y_i.

questions.questionText: The Backward Difference Operator Nabla operating on y_1 is defined as:
questions.explanation: The backward difference Nabla y_i = y_i - y_(i-1).

questions.questionText: The Shift Operator E operating on y_i produces:
questions.explanation: The shift operator shifts the argument by one interval step h: E y_i = y_(i+1).

questions.questionText: What is the algebraic relationship between the Shift operator E and Forward Difference operator Delta?
questions.explanation: Since E y = y(x + h) = y(x) + Delta y(x) = (1 + Delta) y, we have E = 1 + Delta.

questions.questionText: What is the algebraic relationship between the Shift operator E and Backward Difference operator Nabla?
questions.explanation: Nabla y_i = y_i - y_(i-1) = (1 - E^(-1)) y_i, so Nabla = 1 - E^(-1).

questions.questionText: The Central Difference Operator delta operating on y_i is defined as:
questions.explanation: The central difference delta y_i = y_(i + 1/2) - y_(i - 1/2) = (E^(1/2) - E^(-1/2)) y_i.

questions.questionText: The Averaging Operator mu is defined as:
What is the n-th forward difference Delta^n of a polynomial of degree n: P_n(x) = a_n * x^n + ...?
questions.explanation: The n-th difference of an n-th degree polynomial is constant: Delta^n P_n(x) = n! * a_n * h^n.

questions.questionText: What is the (n + 1)-th forward difference Delta^(n + 1) of a polynomial of degree n?
questions.explanation: Since the n-th difference of a degree-n polynomial is constant, all subsequent differences are zero: Delta^(n+1) P_n(x) = 0.

questions.questionText: What is the value of Delta (c) where 'c' is an invariant constant?
questions.explanation: For constant c, Delta c = c - c = 0.
